content_voiceover: This table addresses a critical safety issue with emicizumab, the bispecific antibody used for hemophilia A prophylaxis. Emicizumab mimics factor VIII by bridging factor IXa and factor X, but patients can still have breakthrough bleeds that require additional hemostatic treatment, and one option is activated prothrombin complex concentrate, or aPCC. The problem is that combining emicizumab with aPCC can trigger thrombotic microangiopathy or frank thrombosis, because both agents are driving thrombin generation through overlapping mechanisms. This table breaks down 130 treatment instances of aPCC in 37 patients already on emicizumab, stratified by average daily dose and duration of exposure. Look at the boxed cells on the right, when the average aPCC dose exceeds 100 units per kilogram per 24 hours, adverse events start appearing, and the risk climbs further when that high dose is sustained beyond 48 hours, with 3 TMA cases and thrombotic events clustering there. The take-home safety rule, highlighted at the bottom, is that five of thirteen treatment instances developed TMA or thrombosis specifically when cumulative aPCC exceeded 100 units per kilogram per 24 hours for 24 hours or more.
keypoints: Emicizumab plus aPCC for breakthrough bleeding can trigger thrombotic microangiopathy
Risk clusters when average aPCC dose exceeds 100 units per kilogram per 24 hours
Sustaining that high dose beyond 48 hours further raises thrombotic and TMA risk
Guidance is to avoid aPCC above 100 units per kilogram per 24 hours in emicizumab patients
keypoint_voiceover: Board relevant safety point, in patients on emicizumab prophylaxis, avoid using aPCC at doses above 100 units per kilogram per day for 24 hours or longer, since this combination has been linked to thrombotic microangiopathy and thrombosis.
